lessons.title: Seed Sowing Techniques
lessons.body: Sowing seeds correctly is the first step to strong seedlings. In Africa, many farmers lose seeds because they plant too deep or too shallow. For most vegetable seeds like tomatoes, peppers, and onions, sow in nursery trays or seedbeds filled with fine, well-drained soil. A good mix is 2 parts loam soil, 1 part compost, and 1 part sand. Fill trays to the top, firm gently, and water before sowing. Make small holes 0.5 to 1 cm deep using a pencil or stick. Place one seed per hole for large seeds like watermelon, or scatter thinly for small seeds like lettuce. Cover lightly with soil or vermiculite. For direct sowing in seedbeds, make shallow furrows 1-2 cm deep, spaced 10-15 cm apart. Sow seeds evenly, then cover and water with a fine spray. In hot climates, sow in the evening to reduce evaporation. For crops like maize and beans, direct sowing in the field is common: plant 2-3 seeds per hole, 3-5 cm deep, and thin to one plant after germination. Always use fresh, certified seeds for better germination. Treat seeds with fungicide if available, or dust with wood ash to prevent damping-off. Label each tray with crop name and sowing date. Keep the seedbed moist but not waterlogged. In dry areas, use a mulch cover or shade net to conserve moisture. With proper technique, germination rates can reach 80-95%. Remember, shallow sowing is better than deep sowing for small seeds. Test seed viability by soaking in water: good seeds sink, bad ones float. Sow only viable seeds to save space and time.

lessons.title: Depth and Spacing for Different Seeds
lessons.body: The depth you plant a seed and the space you give it determine whether it germinates and grows well. A simple rule: plant seeds at a depth of 2 to 3 times their diameter. For small seeds like lettuce, carrots, and onions, that means just 0.5 cm deepâbarely covered. For medium seeds like tomatoes, peppers, and cabbage, sow 1 cm deep. For large seeds like maize, beans, and watermelon, plant 3-5 cm deep. If you plant too deep, the seed runs out of energy before reaching light. Too shallow, and it dries out or gets washed away. Spacing depends on the crop and whether you will transplant. In nursery trays, space seeds 2-3 cm apart in all directions. In seedbeds, sow in rows 10-15 cm apart, with seeds 1-2 cm apart within the row. For direct sowing in the field, follow recommended spacing: maize 75 cm between rows and 25 cm between plants; beans 50 cm by 20 cm; tomatoes 60 cm by 60 cm after transplanting. Proper spacing reduces competition for water, nutrients, and light, and lowers disease risk. In Africa, many farmers plant too densely, leading to weak, spindly seedlings. Use a measuring stick or string to keep rows straight and spacing uniform. For crops like groundnuts, plant 5 cm deep and 10 cm apart in rows 45 cm apart. Always firm the soil after sowing to ensure good seed-soil contact. If soil is dry, water after sowing. In sandy soils, plant slightly deeper; in clay soils, shallower. Mark your rows with sticks and labels. After germination, thin seedlings to the correct spacing to avoid overcrowding. Thinning is essential for crops like carrots and beetroot. With correct depth and spacing, you get uniform, healthy seedlings ready for transplanting or growing on.

lessons.title: Germination Requirements: Temperature, Light, Moisture
lessons.body: Seeds need three main things to germinate: the right temperature, enough moisture, and for some, light. In Africa, temperatures vary widely. Most vegetable seeds germinate best between 20Â°C and 30Â°C. Tomatoes, peppers, and eggplant prefer 20-25Â°C. Lettuce germinates poorly above 25Â°Câin hot areas, sow lettuce in cooler months or use shade. Maize and beans germinate well at 25-30Â°C. If it's too cold, seeds rot; too hot, they dry out. Use a thermometer to check soil temperature. Moisture is critical: seeds must absorb water to swell and sprout. Keep the soil consistently moist, like a wrung-out sponge, not soggy. Water gently twice a day in hot weather, once in cool weather. Use a fine rose watering can or spray bottle to avoid washing seeds away. A simple test: squeeze a handful of soilâif water drips, it's too wet; if it crumbles, too dry. Light requirements vary. Most seeds germinate in darkness, but some like lettuce, celery, and coleus need light to germinate. For those, sow on the surface and press lightly, do not cover with soil. Others like onions and leeks germinate better in light. Check seed packets for light needs. In general, cover seeds that need darkness with soil or vermiculite. After germination, all seedlings need bright light to grow strong. In Africa, use shade nets (50% shade) for young seedlings to prevent scorching, but remove shade after 3-4 days for most crops. Ventilation is also important to prevent fungal diseases. If germinating indoors, use a fan or open window. Keep a record of temperature and moisture for each batch. Adjust by using mulch to cool soil, or plastic covers to warm it. With the right conditions, germination occurs in 3-14 days depending on crop. Don't let seeds dry out at this stageâit's the most vulnerable time.

lessons.title: Using Germination Covers and Mats
lessons.body: Germination covers and mats help you control temperature and moisture, leading to faster, more uniform sprouting. In Africa, where temperatures can be extreme, these tools are especially useful. A germination cover is any material placed over the seed tray or bed to retain moisture and warmth. Common covers include clear plastic film, damp burlap, newspaper, or banana leaves. Plastic film is cheap and effective: it traps heat and moisture, creating a mini-greenhouse. Use it in cooler weather or for seeds that need warmth, like peppers and eggplant. However, remove the cover as soon as seedlings emerge, or they will become leggy and prone to disease. In hot climates, use shade cloth or a light mulch as a cover to keep soil cool and moist. For example, in the Sahel, farmers cover seedbeds with millet stalks to reduce evaporation. Germination mats are heated mats placed under seed trays to provide bottom heat. They are useful for germinating heat-loving seeds in cold weather or high-altitude areas. You can make a simple mat by placing a black plastic sheet in the sun to absorb heat, then placing trays on it. Or use a hot water bottle under a tray. Commercial heat mats are available but expensive; a cheaper option is to place trays on a warm compost pile. Always monitor temperature: most seeds need 20-30Â°C. If using plastic covers, check daily for condensationâif too wet, open for a few hours to prevent mold. Remove covers once 50% of seeds have sprouted. After removal, ensure good light and air movement. In humid areas, avoid plastic covers entirely; use shade nets instead. For small-scale farmers, a simple low tunnel made of sticks and clear plastic works well. Remember, covers and mats are tools to mimic ideal conditions. They save water, speed up germination, and protect seeds from heavy rain and pests. But they require daily attention. With proper use, you can achieve over 90% germination even in harsh conditions.

lessons.title: Transplanting Sprouted Seeds
lessons.body: Transplanting is moving young seedlings from the nursery to the main field or larger containers. Do it when seedlings have 2-4 true leaves, usually 2-4 weeks after sowing. In Africa, the best time is early morning or late afternoon to avoid heat stress. Before transplanting, water the nursery thoroughly to loosen roots and reduce shock. Prepare the main field by ploughing and adding compost or manure. Make planting holes the same depth as the seedling's root ball. Handle seedlings by the leaves, not the stem, to avoid damage. Use a small trowel or stick to lift the seedling with its root ball intact. Place it in the hole, fill with soil, and press gently around the base. Water immediately after transplanting. For crops like tomatoes, plant deeper than they were in the nurseryâbury the stem up to the first leaves to encourage roots. Space according to crop: cabbage 45 cm apart, tomatoes 60 cm, peppers 45 cm. In dry areas, transplant in the evening and provide shade for 2-3 days using leaves or shade nets. If the sun is intense, create a small shade using a piece of cardboard or banana leaf. Avoid transplanting on windy days. After transplanting, water daily for the first week, then reduce to every 2-3 days. Mulch around plants to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. If seedlings are leggy, pinch off the lower leaves and plant deeper. For crops that don't transplant well, like carrots and okra, sow directly. Transplanting allows you to select the strongest seedlings and gives them a head start. It also saves water and seeds. But it causes transplant shock, so minimize root disturbance. With care, survival rate can be over 95%. Always keep a few extra seedlings in the nursery as replacements. Record transplanting date and crop for future planning.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Germination Problems
lessons.body: When seeds fail to germinate, don't guessâcheck the common causes. First, test seed viability: soak seeds in water; those that float are usually dead. If less than 70% sink, buy new seeds. Second, check moisture: seeds need constant moisture, but not waterlogging. If soil is dry, water gently; if soggy, improve drainage by adding sand or compost. Third, temperature: if it's too cold (below 15Â°C), seeds may rot. Use a germination mat or cover with plastic to warm. If too hot (above 35Â°C), shade and water more. Fourth, depth: seeds planted too deep run out of energy. Re-sow shallower. Fifth, light: some seeds need light to germinateâif you covered them, remove the cover. Sixth, pests and diseases: ants, crickets, and birds eat seeds. Use netting or sow in trays. Damping-off fungus causes seedlings to collapse; prevent by using clean soil, avoiding overwatering, and improving air flow. If you see mold, remove affected seedlings and treat with cinnamon powder or fungicide. Seventh, soil crusting: heavy clay soils form a hard crust that seedlings can't break through. Break the crust gently with a fork or cover with a thin layer of sand. Eighth, salinity: in coastal areas, salty soil prevents germination. Leach with fresh water or use raised beds. Ninth, old seeds: germination drops after 1-2 years. Store seeds in a cool, dry place in airtight containers. Tenth, wrong sowing time: some seeds need specific seasons. For example, lettuce germinates poorly in hot weather. Sow in cooler months or use shade. If you still have problems, try a simple germination test: place 10 seeds on a wet paper towel in a plastic bag, keep warm, and check after 5-7 days. Count how many sprout. This tells you if the seeds are good. Keep a notebook of what you sow, when, and results. That way, you learn what works on your farm. With patience and observation, you can solve most germination issues.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sowing depth for small seeds like lettuce?
quiz.explanation: Small seeds should be sown very shallow, about 0.5 cm deep, as they have limited energy to reach the surface.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for watering newly sown seeds without washing them away?
quiz.explanation: A fine rose watering can delivers water gently, preventing seeds from being displaced.

quiz.q: Why should you sow seeds in the evening in hot climates?
quiz.explanation: Sowing in the evening reduces water loss through evaporation, keeping seeds moist longer.

quiz.q: What is the rule for planting depth based on seed size?
quiz.explanation: A general rule is to plant seeds at a depth of 2 to 3 times their diameter.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for maize in the field?
quiz.explanation: Maize is typically spaced 75 cm between rows and 25 cm between plants.

quiz.q: Why is proper spacing important for seedlings?
options: A) Reduces competition for water and nutrients
B) Makes the field look neat
quiz.explanation: Proper spacing reduces competition for resources and lowers disease risk.

quiz.q: Which seeds need light to germinate?
quiz.explanation: Lettuce seeds require light to germinate and should be sown on the surface.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for germinating most vegetable seeds?
quiz.explanation: Most vegetable seeds germinate best between 20Â°C and 30Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you test if soil moisture is right for sowing?
options: A) Squeeze a handful; it should form a ball but not drip
B) It should be dry and crumbly
C) It should be dripping wet
D) It should be hard and compact
quiz.explanation: Soil should be moist like a wrung-out sponge, forming a ball without dripping water.

quiz.q: What should you do if seeds are sown too deep?
quiz.explanation: Seeds planted too deep may run out of energy, so it's best to re-sow at the correct depth.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a germination cover?
options: A) To retain moisture and warmth
quiz.explanation: Germination covers help maintain moisture and temperature for better sprouting.

quiz.q: When should you remove a plastic cover from seed trays?
options: A) As soon as seedlings emerge
quiz.explanation: Remove the cover once seedlings emerge to prevent leggy growth and disease.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to a commercial heat mat?
options: A) Placing trays on a warm compost pile
B) Putting trays in a fridge
quiz.explanation: A warm compost pile generates heat and can be used as a natural germination mat.

quiz.q: In hot climates, what can be used as a germination cover to cool soil?
quiz.explanation: Shade cloth reduces heat and moisture loss in hot conditions.

quiz.q: When is the best time to transplant seedlings?
options: A) Early morning or late afternoon
quiz.explanation: Transplanting during cooler parts of the day reduces heat stress and transplant shock.

quiz.q: How should you handle seedlings when transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Handle seedlings by the leaves to avoid damaging the delicate stem.

quiz.q: For tomatoes, how deep should you transplant?
options: A) Bury the stem up to the first leaves
D) Leave the root ball on the surface
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes can be planted deeper to encourage additional root growth.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Watering immediately after transplanting helps settle the soil and reduce shock.

quiz.q: Why is it important to water the nursery before transplanting?
options: A) To loosen roots and reduce shock
quiz.explanation: Watering before transplanting makes it easier to lift seedlings with intact root balls.

quiz.q: Which crop is best sown directly rather than transplanted?
quiz.explanation: Carrots have a taproot and do not transplant well, so they are sown directly.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of seeds not germinating?
quiz.explanation: Planting too deep is a common mistake that prevents germination.

quiz.q: How can you test seed viability?
options: A) Soak in water; good seeds sink
D) Plant them in dry soil
quiz.explanation: Viable seeds are denser and sink in water, while dead seeds float.

quiz.q: What causes damping-off disease in seedlings?
options: A) Overwatering and poor air flow
quiz.explanation: Damping-off is a fungal disease favored by wet, humid conditions and poor ventilation.

quiz.q: What is soil crusting and how does it affect germination?
options: A) A hard surface layer that seedlings can't break through
quiz.explanation: Soil crusting forms a hard layer that impedes seedling emergence.

quiz.q: How can you prevent soil crusting?
options: A) Cover with a thin layer of sand
quiz.explanation: A thin sand layer or organic mulch can prevent crusting and help seedlings emerge.

quiz.q: Why should you store seeds in a cool, dry place?
options: B) To make them grow faster
quiz.explanation: Proper storage preserves seed viability and prevents deterioration.

quiz.q: What is a simple germination test?
options: A) Place seeds on wet paper towel in a plastic bag
quiz.explanation: A paper towel test is a quick way to check germination percentage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on germinating seeds?
options: A) Remove affected seedlings and improve air flow
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates excess moisture; removing affected parts and increasing ventilation helps.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important in germination?
options: A) To learn what works on your farm
quiz.explanation: Records help you track successes and failures for better future planning.

quiz.q: What should you do if seeds fail to germinate due to salinity?
quiz.explanation: Leaching with fresh water helps remove excess salts from the soil.
